item.title: Parenting Considerations for Raising Gifted Children
item.description:
Parenting

Parenting Considerations for Raising Gifted Children

Strategies that will work for your gifted child and family

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Gifted children often face unique challenges, like intensity and perfectionism, not just advantages.
  • There’s no one-size-fits-all curriculum, as giftedness varies widely among individuals.
  • Pressuring gifted kids can worsen perfectionism and dampen their motivation to learn.
Source: Cottonbro Studios / Pexels

Understanding and Accepting That Giftedness Presents Unique Problems

Some parents, grandparents, and other individuals who participate in raising gifted children as they mature into young adulthood may at first believe that exceptionally talented children and teens will be easy to raise because they are so smart, capable, and effective at certain activities. These teachers and caregivers may not be fully informed or experienced in working with certain types of giftedness and the unique challenges that are part of advanced learners’ approach to schooling.

From my own graduate education, teaching, and social experiences with gifted children and older individuals, including my own children, I know that intensity, perfectionism, and idiosyncrasies in social skills create challenges for parents, other caregivers, and teachers. These brave and often frustrated educators need help keeping up with gifted learners. Research on educating prodigies suggests that a progressive school that is accelerated and creative is the most likely to help gifted individuals learn to the best of their abilities. A flexible and complex curriculum and teaching approach will hold the interest of their intellectual and creative minds. A reduction of misbehavior is likely when advanced students are highly engaged in what they are doing.

The Hard Part of Raising Gifted Students

With an enormous amount of intensity and energy, and a need to understand some of the difficult ideas their teachers and parents are presenting, gifted and talented individuals can be very challenging in many ways. Their curiosity, emotional concerns, physical energy, and specific interests often tire out their teachers, parents, and grandparents. In other words, it is not easy to raise gifted children and work with them as they grow.

Patience and fortitude to get them to understand the importance of what you are teaching take a lot of time. Often, they do not want to follow the rules, go to school, do their homework, or put away their phones. Questions galore about life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness are never over. There is always a new concern that someone needs to help them process—someone who has perspective and endless curiosity themselves.

The parent, teacher, or authority in charge of the class needs to establish what question or problem goes first, no matter how insistent the high-achieving students are about “managing” (taking control of) what is being taught. For example, space travel is of great interest to all children and teenagers but especially gifted learners. When the precocious student is in charge of what they want to learn, chaos can become overwhelming, and learning can become highly dysfunctional. Trying to make current ideas understandable is important but hard to do in a reasonable manner.

What Are the Difficulties Educating Gifted Children and Adolescents?

There is no agreed-upon definition of giftedness. The different areas of giftedness make a precise conceptualization impossible in a realistic sense. In other words, being superior in math will look different than being excellent in music or literature. Athletics and music are not really comparable (because of issues of creativity and the uniqueness of sport) to more academic issues that can be more easily cataloged as “giftedness.”

Everyone—parents, teachers, principals, and professors of education—sees giftedness in different ways. This failure to agree on a definition creates the question, “What is the right curriculum and instruction for gifted learners?” My answer is that there is no one curriculum that works for all gifted children.

It is harmful to push or pressure gifted children and teenagers, as it intensifies their perfectionism. Pressure can cause a child to shut down, stop learning, or burn out their passion.

Further Questions About Educating Gifted Children

1. What is the value of intense acceleration with precocious children?

2. Should gifted children be put together in one class to achieve a higher level of knowledge, or does this limit social-emotional development?

Common Problems for Educators of Gifted Learners to Focus Upon

Intensely bright, creative, and curious learners want answers to their questions right away and in elaborate detail. Pointing out to your passionate child or student that some questions are just too complicated to answer completely and immediately is always helpful and necessary. In fact, it is a very educational (or practical) strategy to teach patience and how learning new things takes time.

I remember that I always asked very complicated questions, and the professors would suggest that my question was for more advanced students. I understand this answer now after many years of frustration. I was a complicated, gifted student who, perhaps the professor wished, would ask fewer questions or be accelerated out of their classroom for another teacher to manage.

Conclusions

Try to learn as much as you can about your gifted son, daughter, or students, always remembering what makes them exceptional and proficient. Don’t let people tell you that so-and-so is not gifted because they don’t like to read or do math, etc. Finding special interests such as classical music, art, science, or sports and developing those interests is an important step toward figuring out how to challenge your child or teenager.

Look to experts for help. Other parents and family members are invaluable. Remember, gifted children are not advanced in every area of their lives. Often, they struggle with schoolwork or find socialization hard. Try to be patient and helpful.

What to Do About Unique Learning Difficulties

1. Treat each student as a unique individual as much as possible. Remember that gifted students are not always high achievers; in fact, they may not like school at all. A talented child might need extra help. A child can be very advanced in one subject, or even just one area of a subject, and not advanced in other subjects. This may even bother them because they don’t understand why everything isn’t at the same level of difficulty.

2. Talk to highly talented learners about the ways they are different from average individuals.

3. Challenge your learner when the challenge will be helpful. A student should be ready to learn the material and have an open mind to achieve the best results. Teaching is an art.

item.title: How Can We Make Love Last?
item.description:
Relationships

How Can We Make Love Last?

Why good timing sparks romance, but time deepens love.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Timing can ignite romantic attraction, but time is essential for developing profound love.
  • What makes love exciting is not always what makes it enduring.
  • When timing becomes everything, people may become restless and continually search for alternatives.

"There is only one serious question. And that is: Who knows how to make love stay?" —Tom Robbins

Time plays a paradoxical role in romantic life. Every moment with a beloved can feel precious, yet romantic intensity often wanes as relationships endure. This apparent contradiction points to two important truths: time can deepen love even as it reduces some of its intensity. A crucial step in resolving this paradox is to distinguish between timing and time. Timing can be pivotal for romantic intensity; time is foundational for romantic profundity.

Timing Is Not Everything

"When my soul was in the lost-and-found, you came along to claim it." —Carole King

"I married for timing and convenience, I am afraid to say. My spouse will not admit it, but he did as well." —A married woman

We often hear that timing is everything in life and love. Yet the reality is more nuanced. Timing concerns the particular moment and circumstances in which something happens; time, by contrast, refers to duration, repetition, and development. Timing can be decisive in bringing people together and igniting attraction. Time becomes increasingly important in developing and sustaining enduring love.

Romantic timing may involve sheer luck. Two future lovers happen to meet on a train, at a party, or while traveling. The awareness that they could easily have missed each other can make their encounter seem extraordinarily fortunate. But timing may also involve skill: recognizing and responding to the right circumstances at the right moment. In both cases, timing concerns relatively brief periods. Sometimes, a single decision can alter the course of a relationship. Timing is particularly important in generating intense sexual experiences. This may help explain why quickies, makeup sex, and breakup sex can be remarkably passionate: sexual desire is highly sensitive to circumstances, novelty, emotional states, and timing.

Initial sexual timing is complicated. One view holds that sexual compatibility should be tested as early as possible; another suggests that some sexual restraint allows other dimensions of the relationship to develop first. Research has found associations between slower sexual progression and certain positive relationship outcomes, although these findings are more nuanced than the simple claim that "waiting is better." For example, Busby et al. (2010) found that the speed of entering a sexual relationship was negatively associated with marital quality among women, but not men, while Sassler et al. (2012) similarly found that sexual timing was related to relationship outcomes in complex ways.

The benefits of waiting often depend less on the passage of time itself than on what occurs during that period, such as the development of trust, intimacy, and mutual understanding. As one woman said, "I don't have a set time frame, but it's always before it gets super serious. I got to test drive the car before buying it." There is indeed evidence that resisting immediate temptation for larger later gratification predicts various advantages, including health-related ones (Yanaoka et al., 2022).

Sexual Passion
Source: pexels-15113435-6394845

These considerations can be understood in light of the crucial role of time in enduring romantic love. We can reasonably say, "I have a headache and am not in the mood for sex." It would sound strange to say, "I have a headache and am not in the mood to love you." Sexual desire is often temporary and situation-dependent. Profound love, by contrast, can endure through fatigue, disappointment, distraction, and even conflict. It exists not merely as a momentary feeling but also as a relatively stable disposition toward the beloved. Sexual desire may disappear for an evening; profound love need not disappear with it.

When timing becomes the supreme romantic concern, lovers may become restless. If romantic opportunities are viewed as dependent on luck and fleeting circumstances, people may continually worry that they are missing something better, or that an unexpected opportunity might threaten their current relationship. Constant searching can undermine the development of profound love, which is characterized by greater stability, trust, and emotional calm.

Romantic love is not a perpetual audition in which partners must continuously prove their worth or outperform potential rivals. Enduring love grows less from constant evaluation than from mutual acceptance and shared growth. No one can achieve the highest score all the time. We often become better partners when we are not constantly being tested and compared.

Yet modern romantic life makes timing unusually salient. Dating apps and social media expose us to a seemingly endless stream of alternatives, creating the impression that a better match may always be within reach. Under such conditions, immediate excitement can easily become the primary measure of romantic value. But excitement and profundity are not the same thing.

Time and Profound Love

"If I could save time in a bottle / The first thing that I'd like to do / Is to save every day till eternity passes away / Just to spend them with you." —Jim Croce

Profound love is not merely discovered; it is gradually constructed through time. Partners develop their relationship through shared activities, repeated interactions, emotional experiences, growing mutual understanding, and the gradual accumulation of memories.

Instant sexual intensity is easier to achieve than romantic profundity. Yet a life centered on pursuing fleeting moments can become exhausting and, ultimately, discouraging. People may repeatedly seek excitement while quietly longing for the calmness and security that enduring love provides.

Profound love also requires responsibility. Lovers face ongoing challenges that may at times seem overwhelming. Sustaining a loving relationship requires investments of time, energy, patience, and emotional resources. Yet these investments often generate something that the pursuit of constant excitement rarely provides: a growing sense of security. Paradoxically, however, this responsibility can foster calmness rather than anxiety. When people recognize that they share responsibility for the future of their relationship, they become less dependent on chance and fleeting opportunities. Their bond need not survive merely because the right moment happens to occur; they can actively contribute to its endurance.

Calmness can then become self-reinforcing. The more secure people feel about their relationship's future, the more willing they are to invest in it. Greater investment, in turn, can strengthen the relationship and make its future seem more secure. This helps explain why qualities such as gratitude, compassion, contentment, humility, kindness, and forgiveness are so important for profound love. These virtues may appear less exciting than passion and novelty, but they are often more important for sustaining a loving relationship. In an achievement-oriented culture that celebrates excitement, novelty, and immediate gratification, we can easily underestimate the quiet virtues that enable love to last.

Perhaps this is one of love's deepest paradoxes: what makes love exciting is not always what makes it durable.

Concluding Thoughts

"I'll love you twice as much tomorrow." —Leo Sayer

"Forever and a day, that's how long I'll be loving you." —Kelly Rowland

How can we make love stay? There is no simple answer. Romantic longevity depends upon personal characteristics, relationship dynamics, and changing circumstances. Still, distinguishing between timing and time provides an important clue.

Good timing can bring two people together. It can spark attraction, desire, and the exhilarating sense that something special has begun. But timing alone cannot sustain a loving relationship. That requires time: time to build trust, weather difficulties, create shared memories, and develop a deep understanding of one another. Both romantic intensity and romantic profundity matter. The mistake is to assume that the former can do the work of the latter. We cannot make love stay simply by recreating one exciting moment after another. If there is a secret to making love last, it may be this: stop searching for the perfect moment and start building a love that grows stronger across time.

This post is partly based on my book, The Arc of Love.
